passage:
Monday night. I woke up thirsty at five and saw the kitchen light on. My father Imran was standing there in his vest, rolling rotis for my tiffin, yawning so hard his eyes were wet. I never knew he did that. I always thought the tiffin just appeared.
At lunch I opened the box and my roti was shaped like a star with a little tomato heart. Something went warm in my tummy, and I felt a bit bad that I once said "not this sabzi again."
When I got home I said, "Papa, thanks for the star roti. I saw you at five." He looked shy and said, "Eat well, Sahil." Next week I'll wake up and help.
Sahil

qa.q: What was the shape of the roti in Sahil's tiffin?
qa.a: A star with a little tomato heart.

qa.q: How did Sahil feel when opening the tiffin box at lunch?
qa.a: Warm inside, and a bit guilty about once complaining about the sabzi.

qa.q: What did Sahil do that turned noticing into thanks?
qa.a: Sahil thanked Papa for the star roti, said Sahil had seen him at five, and planned to wake up and help next week.

qa.q: How might Imran feel when Sahil thanks him?
qa.a: Shy and pleased. He looks shy and tells Sahil to eat well, so the thanks clearly matters even though he does not say much. 🙂

grounding: A child begins to see the effort behind a parent's cooking and says so.

passage:
In the village school, Keerthana Madam had shown the class how to add fractions three times, and Zubin still did not get it. He watched her draw the same pie on the board a fourth time, chalk dust on her blue sari, her voice as calm as the first time.
Suddenly he saw it. She could have shouted, and she never did. She had stayed after the bell most days to help slow ones like him, and her sandals were grey with the walk from the next village.
After class he stayed behind. "Madam, thank you for showing us again," he said. "I know you're tired."
She blinked, then smiled. "Come, one more pie." This time it made sense.

qa.q: How many times had Keerthana Madam shown the class how to add fractions before the fourth pie?
qa.a: Three times.

qa.q: What did Zubin realise about Keerthana as he watched her draw the pie a fourth time?
qa.a: That she could have shouted but stayed calm and patient, and that she gave her time to slow learners, so he felt grateful.

qa.q: What did Zubin do after class that made his gratitude real?
qa.a: He stayed behind and thanked Keerthana Madam for showing them again, saying he knew she was tired.

qa.q: How might Keerthana Madam feel when Zubin thanks her?
qa.a: Surprised and touched. She blinks, smiles and offers one more pie.

grounding: A child begins to see the effort behind a teacher's patience and says so.

subtype: Noticing what was done for you [Actor]
passage:
Selin, ten, usually grabbed her lunchbox from the kitchen counter in their Berlin flat and ran. But on Tuesday she woke early for a school trip and found her dad, Yosef, already up at five-thirty, flour on his sleeves, kneading dough for her sandwiches before his early shift at the depot. He yawned between every fold.
She stood in the doorway for a while. She had never thought about when the bread got made.
That afternoon, eating her sandwich on the bus, she noticed the crust was still soft. At dinner she said, "Papa, I saw you making the bread this morning. You looked so tired. Thank you."
Yosef stopped with his fork halfway to his mouth. Then he smiled so widely his eyes crinkled.

qa.q: What time was Yosef already up?
qa.a: At five-thirty.

qa.q: What was Selin feeling as she stood in the doorway?
qa.a: Selin felt surprised and touched, realising for the first time how much effort went into her bread.

qa.q: What made Selin's thank-you meaningful?
qa.a: It named the specific effort she had seen, the early bread-making and how tired he looked, rather than a general thanks.

qa.q: How did Yosef feel when Selin thanked him?
qa.a: Yosef was surprised and deeply pleased, smiling so widely his eyes crinkled.

grounding: Shows a child noticing the effort behind a parent's early-morning cooking and thanking him for it.

In Class 5, Irfan had always thought Damini Ma'am's job was easy: talk, write on the board, go home. Then, on Wednesday, he stayed back to finish his map and watched her with Bablu, who still couldn't do long division.
She explained it once. Bablu shook his head. She drew it with beans. He shook his head again. She tried coins, then a story about sharing mangoes. The fourth time, Bablu's face lit up. Damini Ma'am didn't sigh once. Irfan noticed her tea had gone cold on the desk.
On his way out, Irfan hesitated at the door. "Ma'am, you explained that four times. That's really patient. Thanks for helping Bablu." Damini Ma'am looked up, surprised, and her tired face softened.

qa.q: What did Damini Ma'am use the second time?
qa.a: Beans.

qa.q: How did Irfan feel about the teacher after watching her with Bablu?
qa.a: Irfan had thought her job was easy, but he felt a new respect and appreciation after seeing her patience.

qa.q: What made Irfan's thank-you meaningful?
qa.a: It named exactly what he had noticed: explaining four times without sighing.

qa.q: How might Damini Ma'am feel hearing Irfan's words?
qa.a: She was surprised and touched, her tired face softening at being noticed.

grounding: Shows a child beginning to see the effort behind a teacher's patience and saying so.

subtype: Noticing what was done for you [Actor]
passage:
Monday. Anirban complained that the dinner beans were "boring again". His Dadu, Harish, said nothing.
Thursday. School was off, so Anirban followed Dadu to the rooftop garden at six. He watched Dadu carry twelve buckets of water up the stairs, pick beetles off by hand, and tie up the bean vines with strips of old sari. By eight, Dadu's shirt was soaked.
Saturday. There were beans again at dinner. Anirban ate a mouthful slowly. "Dadu, these are from the fourth row, right? The ones you tied up?" Dadu nodded. "They're good. Thank you for carrying all that water." Dadu laughed and put an extra spoonful on his plate.

qa.q: How many buckets of water did Dadu carry up?
qa.a: Twelve buckets.

qa.q: How did Anirban feel about the beans on Saturday compared with Monday?
qa.a: On Monday he was bored and complained; by Saturday he felt grateful, having seen the work behind them.

qa.q: What helped Anirban's gratitude grow?
qa.a: Seeing the work himself on Thursday, rather than being lectured, let him notice the effort.

qa.q: How might Harish Dadu have felt when Anirban complained on Monday?
qa.a: Harish Dadu may have felt a little hurt but chose to say nothing.

grounding: Shows a child's gratitude growing from noticing the effort behind a grandparent's food, not from a lecture.

passage:
"Mehak, you asked why I always thank your Dadi for the rotis. Let your Baljeet Dadaji tell you when it started.
"I was nine, in our village near Moga. Every morning I woke up to hot makki di roti and never thought about it. My father kept telling me, 'You're lucky, you know. Many boys don't eat like this.' I just rolled my eyes.
"Then one winter night I couldn't sleep and came down to the kitchen at five. My mother was already there, in the cold, grinding the maize flour by hand, blowing on the chulha to get it going. Her fingers were cracked.
"Nobody had to lecture me after that. At breakfast I said, 'Bebe, you got up in the dark for this.' She stopped and looked at me like I'd given her a gift.
"From then on, I noticed. That's all gratitude is, Mehak. Noticing.

qa.q: What was young Baljeet's mother doing in the kitchen at five?
qa.a: She was grinding the maize flour by hand, blowing on the chulha to get it going.

qa.q: What was young Baljeet feeling when he saw his mother's cracked fingers?
qa.a: Young Baljeet felt moved and a little ashamed, suddenly seeing the effort behind the rotis he had taken for granted.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and why did it matter more than the lectures?
qa.a: Seeing his mother working in the cold dark made him notice her effort himself, which grew real gratitude that his father's lectures never did.

qa.q: How did Bebe feel when young Baljeet thanked her?
qa.a: Bebe felt touched and surprised, looking at him like he'd given her a gift.

grounding: An elder recalls a child noticing the effort behind a parent's cooking, showing gratitude grows from noticing, not lectures.
